blocks.prompt: The Tail That Can Hold On
blocks.text: A monkey can climb with its hands and its feet. Some monkeys can climb with their tail too. The tail wraps around a branch and holds tight. It is strong enough to hold the whole monkey in the air. Then both hands are free. The monkey can pick fruit while it hangs upside down. The tip of the tail has no fur on one side. That bare patch grips the branch, the way your bare foot grips a wet floor. Not every monkey can do this. The ones that can live in the warm forests of South America.

blocks.prompt: The Fifth Hand
blocks.text: Hold your arm out and count your limbs. Two arms, two legs. A spider monkey has four limbs too, and then it has one more. Its tail works like a fifth hand. A spider monkey's tail is longer than its body. The last part of the underside has no fur at all. That naked patch is covered in tiny ridges, like the ones on your fingertips, and it grips a branch the way your fingers grip a pencil. The tail is strong enough to hold the monkey's whole weight while it reaches for fruit with both hands. It is also careful. A spider monkey can curl the tip of its tail around a single grape and lift it. Here is the strange part. A spider monkey has almost no thumb. Its four long fingers hook over a branch like a coat hanger, so it can swing fast and far without gripping. The hand gave up its thumb. The tail took over the job.

blocks.prompt: Two Kinds of Monkey, One Kind of Tail
blocks.text: Split every monkey on Earth into two groups and you can do it with a map. New World monkeys live in the forests of Central and South America. Old World monkeys live in Africa and Asia. The two groups have been apart for tens of millions of years, and it shows. Look at the nose first. A New World monkey's nostrils sit far apart and open out to the sides. An Old World monkey's nostrils sit close together and point down, like yours. Scientists sorted the two groups this way long before they had any other test. Now look at the tail. Some New World monkeys have a prehensile tail, which means a tail that can grip. Spider monkeys, howler monkeys, woolly monkeys, and capuchins all use theirs to hold on. Not one Old World monkey can do it. A baboon or a macaque can wave its tail and balance with it, but it cannot hang from it. Why the difference? Nobody is certain. The best guess is about the forest itself. New World monkeys spend almost their whole lives up in the branches, where a spare grip is worth the trouble of growing one. Many Old World monkeys travel on the ground as well, walking on all fours between trees, and a gripping tail buys them less. One more thing worth knowing. Chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans, and gibbons are not monkeys at all. They are apes, and no ape has a tail. Neither does a human. If you ever want to tell a monkey from an ape at the zoo, look behind it.

blocks.prompt: The Tail That Evolved Twice
blocks.text: Around 35 million years ago, a small group of monkeys arrived in South America. Nobody saw them come. The best evidence says they drifted across the Atlantic from Africa on a raft of storm-torn trees and matted vegetation, at a time when the ocean was narrower than it is now. It sounds absurd. It is also the only explanation that fits the fossils and the genes. What they found was a continent of forest and no competition. Their descendants, the New World monkeys, spread through the canopy and stayed there. And in that canopy, something remarkable happened twice. The first group to manage it was the atelids: spider monkeys, howler monkeys, woolly monkeys, and muriquis. Their tails became true fifth limbs. The underside of the tip lost its fur entirely and grew a pad ribbed with fine ridges, the same kind of ridges that make your fingerprints. Beneath the skin, the tail is packed with touch receptors, and the brain gives it a generous share of its map of the body, the way your brain devotes an outsized area to your hands. A spider monkey does not merely hook its tail over a branch. It feels the branch through its tail. The second group was the capuchins, and they are not close cousins of the atelids. Their tail grips too, but it kept its fur and has no ridged pad. It works, and it works differently. Two separate lineages, in the same forest, solved the same problem in their own way. Biologists call that convergent evolution, and it is one of the strongest hints that a trait is genuinely useful rather than an accident of family history. Which raises the obvious question: why has no Old World monkey ever grown one? Africa and Asia have plenty of forest and plenty of monkeys. The likeliest answer is that a gripping tail pays only if you almost never come down. Baboons, macaques, and vervets move on the ground as well as in the trees, and a tail built for hanging is expensive to grow and useless on a plain. Evolution does not reward a tool you rarely pick up. So the fifth hand is not a monkey feature. It is a New World feature, invented twice, in one forest, by animals whose ancestors got there by accident.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Prehensile tails evolved at least twice
Atelid tail pads carry ridges, like fingerprints
Capuchin tails grip but keep their fur
Apes lost their tails about 25 million years ago
TBXT: the gene linked to ape tail loss
Monkeys rafted to South America across the Atlantic

blocks.prompt: The Fifth Hand: How a Tail Became a Limb
blocks.text: Start with an accident. Roughly 35 million years ago, a few small primates washed up on the coast of South America, almost certainly carried from Africa on a mat of storm-wrecked vegetation across an Atlantic narrower than today's. It is an absurd way to colonize a continent, and the fossils and the genetics agree that it is what happened. The passengers found an unbroken forest and almost no rivals in it. Their descendants, the New World monkeys, climbed into the canopy and, in a sense, never came back down. Life in the canopy sets a hard problem. Every meal is at the end of a branch too thin to stand on, and every mistake is a long fall. A monkey needs to reach out while still holding on. Four limbs make that a trade: let go with one hand and you lose a third of your grip. At least two separate lineages of New World monkey solved the problem the same way, by promoting the tail. The atelids went furthest. Spider monkeys, howler monkeys, woolly monkeys, and muriquis carry a tail longer than the rest of the body, driven by extra vertebrae, thickened muscle, and heavy tendons. The underside of the tip is bare. It carries a pad of ridged skin with the same looping patterns that give you fingerprints, and it is dense with touch receptors. In the brain, the region that receives signals from that pad is disproportionately large, arranged much as the region for your hand is arranged in yours. This is what separates a fifth limb from a hook. A spider monkey can hang its full weight from its tail, and it can also curl the tip around a single grape and lift it without crushing it. The tail is not just strong. It is skilled. The capuchins arrived at a gripping tail independently, and they built a different one. It stayed furred, it has no friction pad, and it wraps and anchors rather than manipulates. Capuchins are not close relatives of the atelids, which makes this a textbook case of convergent evolution: two lineages, one forest, one problem, two answers that are not copies of each other. When a trait shows up twice by separate routes, that is strong evidence it is being built by the environment rather than inherited by chance. The obvious control experiment is on the other side of the world, and it comes out negative. Africa and Asia have enormous forests and hundreds of monkey species, and not one of them has a prehensile tail. Baboons, macaques, and vervets balance with their tails, signal with them, and nothing more. The likeliest explanation is a cost calculation. A gripping tail is expensive: extra bone, extra muscle, extra nerve, all of it carried everywhere for life. It pays only for an animal that essentially never leaves the branches. Old World monkeys forage on the ground routinely, and for them the tail would be a tool bought at full price and rarely used. Apes went the other way entirely. Chimpanzees, gorillas, orangutans, gibbons, and humans have no tail at all. In 2024, researchers reported a likely reason: a stray piece of DNA that inserted itself into a gene called TBXT in a common ancestor of the apes, roughly 25 million years ago. When they engineered the same insertion into mice, the mice were born with shortened tails or none. One accident of copy-and-paste, and a whole branch of the primate family lost its tail forever. So look at the two ends of the story. One group of primates spent millions of years turning a tail into a hand. Another lost the tail in what may have been a single genetic slip. Neither outcome was planned. Both are still walking around.
